This ryokan‑style home looks straight out of Japan — but it’s an EC in Singapore
article:
Japanese influences run throughout Miya and Jason's three-bedroom-plus-study unit at the North Gaia executive condo (EC) in Yishun.

Shoji- inspired panels line parts of the home, all three bedrooms have sliding doors, and a stone lantern greets visitors at the entrance.

On the balcony, the family eats around a low dining table in a setting that reminds the homeowners of the old-school Japanese restaurants from their travels.

Elsewhere, there is a cosy corner underneath a loft bed for their 10-year-old son to read and play.

The 1,076 sq ft home houses Miya, 41, an accountant, her husband Jason, 39, an army regular, and their son, Mikael. The family moved into the apartment in January this year, following an $80,000 renovation that included electrical works.

In love with all things Japan

For the couple, the Japanese references are personal. They travel to Japan regularly, so much so that Miya says her colleagues call the country her "second home".

When it came to their own home, they wanted to recreate some of that feeling without losing sight of the practical needs of a family of three.

"We are very chill," Miya says. "I need a home that feels cosy and comfortable."

But cosy does not mean dark and sleepy — Miya says she still needs light that is bright enough to be able to work at home and for her son to do his homework in the different spaces.

Storage was another priority, as the family owns plenty of clothes, shoes, jewellery and other belongings, and Miya wanted as much of it as possible tucked away.

"We need a lot of storage to hide [our belongings] so that we don't see the mess," she says.

A decade to figure out what they want

Before North Gaia, the family lived in a four-room HDB flat for about a decade. It was Miya and Jason's first home together, and Jason was working overseas when it was being put together.

Miya describes the process as “largely DIY”. Family members helped with the painting, and she had little idea then of what she wanted.

"I didn't know what to do," she recalls. "I was completely easygoing with the renovation, with help and advice from my family in the construction business. Aesthetics were not even a consideration back then."

Living there for 10 years gave the couple a clearer idea of what they wanted from their next home.

As a result, when they bought their second home, Miya had a list of priorities for the renovation: good lighting, extensive storage, no wasted corners and a consistent Japanese-inspired interior.

She was also approaching this EC unit’s renovation with a much longer horizon.

"I don't wish to move anymore in my entire life. Due to the amount of things we have, I hate shifting houses. I plan to stay here forever, [so] I decided to get a proper interior designer," she says.

She adds with a laugh that her husband had even become increasingly exasperated by the search for an interior designer, as Miya’s expectations were high.

The couple met around 10 interior designers before settling on one: Yang’s Inspiration Design.

Memory of Kusatsu

Miya knew she wanted a Japanese-inspired home, but one of the clearest references came from a family trip to Kusatsu Onsen in Japan.

They struggled to find their way to the remote town, getting lost in the dark and snow. By the time they finally arrived, they were exhausted.

Stepping into the ryokan , a traditional Japanese inn, and soaking in the onsen after the difficult journey left an impression on Miya. “It was the best thing after a hectic day,” she recalls.

It was that sense of relief and calm that the couple wanted to recreate at home: a place where they could leave the bustle of the day behind once they stepped through the door.

When Miya was choosing an interior designer, she met with around 10 firms and compared their proposals for the home. While many had similar ideas for the main living area, Dexter Lim from Yang’s Inspiration Design stood out for his treatment of the corridor, which reminded her of that experience in Kusatsu.

“The corridor vibes he gave me were the exact same as what I had felt at the onsen ,” she says.

Finding room for everything

The family did not make major changes to the unit's original layout. Much of the work instead involved making better use of the space available.

"I need a lot of custom carpentry," says Miya. "We want to utilise all corners and don't want any dead space."

At the foyer, she had two requirements: a place for their Japanese stone lantern, and a privacy screen of sorts that would prevent passersby from looking directly into the unit when the front door was open.

The three bedrooms, meanwhile, were fitted with sliding doors. The Shoji -inspired panels carry the Japanese reference further into the interior.

Miya and Jason have also accumulated a sizeable collection of figurines, given their interest in anime. Miya felt the colourful collection would compete with the rest of the interior, so most of it was given a home of its own in the games room.

"My figurines don't exactly match the theme of my house, so they must be hidden in the room, for my own enjoyment," she says.

Ironically, the room initially meant just to contain the things Miya wanted to keep out of sight has become the space she now uses most.

She works, watches television and plays games there. Since moving in January 2026, she estimates she has slept in the master bedroom fewer than four nights.

"I spend more time there than my master bedroom," she admits.

A room that can grow with their son

Their son's bedroom was likewise planned for the long run.

The 10-year-old initially gravitated towards brighter colours, including blue, but his parents ultimately made the design decisions.

"Mikael’s room needs to be designed in a way so he won’t be embarrassed to bring his friends home, be it when he’s 10 or 20," she says.

A loft bed frees up the floor space below to create a cosy nook for him to read and play with his toys.

Dinners at the balcony

Instead of trying to squeeze a dining area into the main living space, Miya and Jason made use of the balcony, which might otherwise have served as a laundry area.

With its low, sit-down arrangement, the space unexpectedly took on another Japanese reference. To Miya, it resembles the traditional restaurants in Japan. "Once you sit down, you won't wish to stand back up," she says.

There is no room in the house she considers her favourite. She works and unwinds in the games room, and the family gathers for meals on the balcony.  “I love every single part of the house!” she exclaims, reiterating her hope that this will be their forever home.

title: Frasers Hospitality opens Fraser Place Roppongi, Tokyo
article:
Frasers Hospitality, a business unit of Frasers Property, has announced the opening of Fraser Place Roppongi, Tokyo, expanding its presence in Japan.

Located in the Minato district, the serviced residence offers 172 rooms ranging from studios to one- and two-bedroom apartments. Each residence has a kitchenette, an in-room washing machine and complimentary WiFi.

Guests also have access to a residents’ lounge and co-working hub, an indoor gym, meeting spaces and a daily breakfast service.

The new property strengthens Frasers Hospitality’s presence in Japan, building on Fraser Residence Nankai Osaka, noted outgoing CEO Eu Chin Fen in an Oct 12 release. Last week, Frasers Hospitality announced she would be stepping down from her role as CEO of Frasers Hospitality , effective Jan 1, 2027.

Eu added that the new property reflects Frasers Hospitality's approach of entering markets with strong international appeal and tailoring its serviced living offerings to each location.

The 114-room Fraser Residence Nakai Osaka opened in 2010. It marked Frasers' first serviced apartment in Japan.

Frasers Hospitality currently has a portfolio of over 100 properties across 19 countries.

In Japan, its properties also include Ana Crowne Plaza Kobe, a 593-room hotel in Kobe City; Estem Court Namba VII Beyond Osaka, a 124-key premium rental apartment; and the 244-key Yotel Tokyo Ginza.

The recent strengthening of the US dollar against the Malaysian ringgit should be positive for Riverstone Holdings (Riverstone), reversing some of the forex headwinds seen earlier in the year.
USD/MYR has moved to around 4.08 in early-Oct 26, compared with the stronger ringgit environment that weighed on Riverstone’s 1H26 earnings.
With a significant portion of sales denominated in US dollars while a large part of its core base is in ringgit, a stronger US dollar should support revenue translations and margins in the near term.

Chinese glovemakers’ ASP hikes improve pricing environment
. Recent price increases by Chinese glove manufacturers are positive for the broader glove pricing environment. Chinese generic nitrile glove ASPs have risen, narrowing their discount to Malaysian producers to around US$0.50/1,000 pieces from US$1.50-2.00 previously.
This gives Malaysian glovemakers greater room to raise ASPs without materially widening the price differential and should support Riverstone’s healthcare glove pricing and margins.

title: Seatrium Launches a S$200 Million Share Buyback: Is the Stock Worth a Look?
article:
Seatrium Limited
(SGX: 5E2) has announced a new
S$200 million share buyback
programme, doubling its latest buyback programme (completed on 1 September 2026), and funded from existing cash.
This latest announcement continues the buybacks Seatrium has already undertaken, making it more important than a one-off announcement.
With shares currently trading around S$2, is this just a capital-return exercise or part of the investment case?
Metric / Area
Summary
Stock Name & Ticker
Seatrium Limited
(SGX: 5E2)
Share Buyback
S$200 million programme funded by cash
Current 2% mandate limits repurchases to ~68 million shares (~S$136 million at S$2/share)
Financial Performance
1H2026 revenue up 5% YoY to to S$5.6 billion
Net profit up 158% to S$373 million (up 54% to S$212 million excluding divestment gains)
Gross margin expanded to 8.6%
Order Book Pipeline
Net order book of of S$13.3 billion across 24 projects through 2033; chasing a pipeline of >S$32 billion
Balance Sheet & Cash Flow
S$3.4 billion liquidity
Net leverage at 0.5x
Gross debt of S$2.4 billion
Underlying 1H2026 free cash flow was -S$11 million excluding asset sales and settlements
Valuation
S$2.00 share price (~S$7.1 billion market cap)
Forward P/E: 13.9x
P/B: 0.9x
What Exactly Has Seatrium Announced?
The buyback’s pace will depend on Seatrium’s share price, market conditions and capital priorities.
This programme runs under a shareholder mandate that allows repurchases of up to 2% of issued shares and requires approval at each annual general meeting.
The first programme launched in April 2024 took about 28 months to complete.
Under that earlier programme, repurchased shares were held as treasury shares.
These treasury shares can be used for employee share plans and directors’ fees, or cancelled against share capital.
This new programme is described as supporting both shareholder returns and employee incentives.
In the first nine months of 2026, Seatrium’s purchases averaged about S$2.12 a share, compared with about S$1.77 for the first repurchase in June 2024.
Why Do Companies Buy Back Their Own Shares?
A buyback enhances shareholder returns alongside
dividends
.
By reducing the shares outstanding, each remaining shareholder owns a bigger slice of the company and earnings per share (EPS) rise if profit holds steady.
It can also signal that management thinks the shares are worth more than the market price, though this is not proof.
Buybacks only create value if the price paid is sensible and the cash isn’t required elsewhere.
Related articles:
Top 3 Temasek-Backed Stocks With Aggressive Share Buybacks
Top 6 Temasek-Backed Stocks With Aggressive Share Buybacks
What Has Been Happening at Seatrium?
Beyond its buyback, what has Seatrium been reporting?
For the six months ended 30 June 2026 (1H2026), revenue rose 5% year on year (YoY) to S$5.6 billion.
Net profit was S$373 million, up 158%, but this figure includes divestment gains.
Excluding divestment gains, net profit rose 54% YoY to S$212 million, helped by gross margin widening from 7.4% to 8.6% on a higher-margin project mix and lower costs.
EBITDA excluding divestments rose 20% YoY to S$479 million.
As of 30 June 2026, Seatrium’s net order book was S$13.3 billion, spanning 24 projects through 2033.
This represents a softening from S$17.8 billion as at 31 December 2025, as work done on existing projects outpaced new orders.
The group is chasing a pipeline of more than S$32 billion and holds a letter of intent from
Golar LNG Limited
(NASDAQ: GLNG) for a third floating LNG conversion, with a contract expected to be signed in 2H2026.
Seatrium’s balance sheet looks healthy, supported by S$3.4 billion in liquidity.
From December 2025, gross debt fell 5% to S$2.4 billion, while net debt held steady at S$680 million.
Net finance costs dropped 20% YoY to S$43 million, while net leverage improved to 0.5x (from 0.8x as at 31 December 2025).
Operationally, it completed its seventh conversion of an LNG carrier into a floating storage regasification unit (FSRU) for Karpowership in September and is pursuing energy-transition work such as offshore wind.
Is the S$200 Million Buyback Material?
S$200 million equals about 2.8% of Seatrium’s S$7.1 billion market value.
At S$2 a share, S$200 million would buy roughly 100 million shares, about 2.9% of the 3.39 billion outstanding.
But the current mandate caps buybacks at 2% of issued shares, roughly 68 million shares or about S$136 million at today’s price.
Spending the rest depends on shareholders renewing the mandate at future AGMs.
If the repurchased shares were cancelled, EPS would rise by a similar percentage, all else being equal.
Shares reissued to employees, however, would not shrink the share count.
Ultimately, a buyback does not guarantee share price appreciation, nor does it replace the need for sustained earnings and cash flow growth.
The Biggest Question: Can Seatrium Generate Enough Cash?
This is the real test.
Excluding a one-off S$73 million legal settlement, operating cash flow for 1H2026 was S$114 million, still thin compared to underlying profit.
Capital expenditure (capex) was S$52 million, mainly on project needs and safety requirements.
Subtracting capex leaves free cash flow (FCF) of roughly negative S$11 million.
Seatrium reported a headline FCF of S$237 million, that figure relied on S$167 million in asset sales.
How Does Seatrium’s Stock Move From Here?
Seatrium must convert new and existing orders into revenue and cash flows while maintaining execution margins.
Watch buyback activity and improving sentiment towards Seatrium’s offshore and marine operations.
The buyback is a reason to look at the stock, not the reason to own it.
What Could Go Wrong?
If projects overrun or are delayed, Seatrium’s margins would take a direct hit.
Large projects also absorb working capital before payments arrive, which could pressure cash flows.
Higher interest rates would raise Seatrium’s financing costs, though the impact would be limited: 64% of its debt was at fixed rates as of 30 June 2026.
Offshore spending is also highly cyclical, which could derail Seatrium’s financial results.
If earnings falter, shares repurchased today could prove to have been expensive.
Is Seatrium’s Stock Cheap After the Buyback Announcement?
As of 9 October 2026, Seatrium’s shares closed at S$2, giving it a market capitalisation of S$7.1 billion.
That values the company at roughly 13.9x forward earnings, with a price-to-book (P/B) ratio at roughly 0.9x.
These
valuations
are within historical ranges.
By comparison,
Yangzijiang Shipbuilding (Holdings) Ltd.
(SGX: BS6) trades at about 2.1x book value.
On these measures, Seatrium’s valuation looks reasonable rather than cheap.
Related articles:
3 Dividend Blue Chips Powering the STI’s 2026 Rally
Which Singapore Marine Stock Is a Better Buy: Yangzijiang or Seatrium?
Get Smart: A Buyback Is a Signal, Not the Investment Case
The S$200 million programme is a bigger commitment than the last and could lift EPS.
But the headline figure is larger than the mandate can deliver at today’s price; first-half free cash flow leaned on asset sales.
The turnaround is real in margins and profit, but still has to show up in operating cash flow and new orders.
The buyback is a reason to look at the stock, not the reason to own it.

article:
Singapore companies have never spent this much buying back their own shares.
Between January and September 2026 (9M2026), 80 primary-listed companies spent S$2.38 billion
repurchasing their stock
on the open market.
That already beats the S$2.23 billion spent in all of 2025, which was itself a record across the 10 years Singapore Exchange (SGX) has tracked.
Look closer and four names stand out.
These four Temasek-linked companies account for S$1.56 billion of this year’s total, or roughly two of every three buyback dollars.

These four buybacks do different jobs for shareholders.
How much has Singtel spent, and what does it get shareholders?
Singapore Telecommunications Limited
(SGX: Z74), or Singtel, spent S$1.05 billion on buybacks in 9M2026, or 44.1% of the market total on its own.
SGX says Singtel’s buyback aims to lift earnings per share.
Singtel has used 41% of its S$2 billion programme.
It has cancelled roughly S$819 million worth of shares, lifting earnings per share by 1.1%.
Alongside the buyback, Singtel has raised around S$6.8 billion towards its S$9 billion asset-recycling target.
For the first quarter of the fiscal year ending 31 March 2027 (1QFY2027), underlying net profit rose 21% year on year (YoY) to S$831 million.
The FY2026 dividend also rose to S$0.185 per share from S$0.170.
The soft spot is at home.
Singtel Singapore’s operating profit slipped 2% YoY amid intense price competition, and group revenue was flat on a constant-currency basis.
Related articles:
DBS, Singtel and ST Engineering Have Rallied: Which Is Still Worth Buying?
Singtel vs ST Engineering: Which Dividend Stock Is Better for the Next 10 Years?
Why would Keppel buy back shares it plans to reuse?
Keppel Ltd
(SGX: BN4) bought back S$364.9 million of shares in 9M2026.
According to SGX, Keppel wants the shares for employee share plans and future acquisitions, so it need not issue new ones.
That avoids diluting existing shareholders, though it does not shrink the overall share count.
The profit picture is messier.
For the first half of 2026 (1H2026), net profit attributable to shareholders fell 59% YoY to S$154.7 million following a S$375 million loss in the non-core portfolio.
Strip that portfolio out, and net profit grew 25% to S$530 million.
Look closely at cash flow here.
Operating cash flow fell to S$96.8 million from S$219.4 million a year ago.
Keppel reported a free cash inflow of S$570 million, but only because of S$1.1 billion of divestment proceeds and dividends received.
As at 30 June 2026, the group held S$2.2 billion of cash against S$11.3 billion of borrowings.
The interim dividend held steady at S$0.150 per share.
Related articles:
Keppel Corporation: Why Analysts Are Overlooking Its Deep Value
Is Sembcorp or Keppel a Better Long-Term Investment for Infrastructure?
Can ST Engineering afford buybacks and a rising dividend?
Singapore Technologies Engineering Ltd (SGX: S63), or ST Engineering, bought back a more modest S$96.6 million in 9M2026.
For the first half of 2026 (1H2026), net profit attributable to shareholders climbed 27.1% YoY to S$512.1 million.
Free cash flow grew to S$591.6 million from S$484.6 million.
Dividends for the half came to S$0.09 per share, up from S$0.08, with plans for another S$0.05 for 3Q2026.
Its order book reached a record S$35.7 billion.
Keep an eye on the cash balance, though.
Cash and cash equivalents dropped to S$255.3 million as at 30 June 2026, down from S$576.4 million at the end of 2025.
Total borrowings, including lease liabilities, stood at S$4.7 billion.
Related articles:
Why Has ST Engineering Become So Much More Valuable? We Went Back Through 10 Years of Results
Yangzijiang vs ST Engineering: Which Singapore Growth Stock Would I Buy?
How does SGX’s buyback sit alongside its dividend?
Singapore Exchange Limited (SGX: S68), or SGX, is the smallest buyer of the four, at S$51.0 million in 9M2026.
Its Temasek link also works differently.
The 23.35% stake sits with SEL Holdings.
In a 2011 statement, Temasek said SEL holds the stake for the Financial Sector Development Fund and cannot vote those shares.
For the fiscal year ended 30 June 2026 (FY2026), adjusted net profit rose 24.6% YoY to S$759.5 million, and free cash flow grew 2.0% to S$788.8 million.
SGX’s FY2026 ordinary dividend came to S$0.445 per share.
On top of that, SGX has proposed a one-off additional dividend of S$0.125 per share.
Together, that brings the payout to S$0.570, compared to S$0.375 a year ago.
Management plans to raise the dividend by 0.25 cents every quarter until FY2028 and to repay its debt in full in FY2027.
Related articles:
3 Singapore Blue-Chip Stocks Hitting 52-Week Highs: Are They Still Buys?
3 Singapore Stocks That Have Raised Their Dividends Consistently Over the Past 5 Years
Get Smart: What should you check before you cheer a buyback?
Start with what happens to the shares.
When Singtel cancels the shares it buys, each remaining share owns a slightly bigger slice of profit.
When Keppel holds shares for staff plans and deals, your slice stays the same size.
Then follow the cash.
Free cash flow
is the lifeblood of dividends, and it pays for buybacks too.
ST Engineering grew free cash flow while it bought back shares.
Keppel leaned on divestments.
A buyback funded by asset sales can slow once the asset sales do.
If you own any of these four, ask one question every results season.
Can free cash flow cover both the
dividend
and the buyback?
If it can, the buyback is working for you.

title: Singapore Bank Shares Have Fallen. Are They Cheap Enough Yet?
article:
Three trading days.
That was all it took for Singapore’s bank shares to give back over two months of gains.
The sell-off began last Wednesday (7 October), and coincided with Citi downgrading
Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation
(SGX: O39), or OCBC, from neutral to sell.
OCBC shares fell by over 5% that day.
DBS Group Holdings
(SGX: D05) and
United Overseas Bank
(SGX: U11), or UOB, fell 1.4% and 2.9% respectively.
By Friday’s close, OCBC shares sat around 11% below their 52-week high. UOB was down by close to 11% and DBS by 7.2%.
If you own bank shares, you don’t need to panic.
As bad as it gets?
The drop feels sharp because it came so fast.
Widen the lens from three days to three months, and DBS and OCBC shares sit roughly where they traded in late July.
The three banks make up 57% of the
Straits Times Index
(SGX: ^STI), or STI.
That index ended Friday only around 7.3% below its 52-week high.
In other words, we’re not at a 10% decline yet, so we’re not in market correction territory — yet.
You shouldn’t be surprised if one comes.
Historically, the STI has fallen by 10% or more in around eight out of every 10 years.
Was Citi right to call OCBC a sell?
Citi expects OCBC’s third-quarter earnings to come in flat year on year after an exceptional second quarter.
It also expects higher fixed deposit rates to squeeze OCBC’s margins, and it questions OCBC’s valuation.
Here’s the thing: before Wednesday’s downgrade, OCBC shares were already far above their typical valuation multiple.
Before Wednesday’s downgrade, investors were paying around 2.3 times book value.
For context, the shares have historically averaged at roughly 1.2 times.
At 2.3 times, the market just needed a reason to sell.
Any reason would do.
All three banks were due for a pullback on valuation alone, whether Citi said so or someone else did.
On Friday (9 October 2026), OCBC traded at around 2.1 times book value.
To put it simply, the shares are cheaper, but they are far from cheap.
Has anything changed inside the banks?
The short answer is no.
The banks last reported in early August, and those numbers still stand.
In the first half of 2026 (1H 2026), OCBC grew total income by 11% year on year to S$8 billion.
Net interest income fell 3% as the bank’s interest margin narrowed from 1.98% a year ago to 1.73% in 1H 2026.
Non-interest income more than made up the gap.
It rose 36% to S$3.51 billion, backed by net fee income, which grew 26% to S$1.41 billion.
OCBC raised its interim ordinary dividend by 15% to S$0.47 per share, representing a payout of 50% of profit.
Management still expects total income to grow in 2026.
It expects net interest income to dip slightly.
On the flip side, the US Federal Reserve raised
interest rates
in September 2026 for the first time since July 2023, a move that could slow the decline in margins over time.
We’ll have to wait for management to comment on its outlook when OCBC reports its next earnings.
What should you watch when the banks report?
The banks should report third-quarter results in late October or early November.
On the lending side, expect net interest margins to keep slipping.
At the same time, you want loan growth to be strong enough to offset that decline.
OCBC currently expects to deliver high-single to low-double-digit loan growth in 2026.
On the non-lending side, watch whether wealth management fees and insurance income keep growing.
Get Smart: Think in years, not quarters
Think beyond the next set of results.
You want any rise in the share price to come from business growth, not just optimism.
Over the
long term
, the business, not the multiple, should drive your returns.
If the business delivers and the share price still falls, you get to buy more of it at a lower multiple.

title: IMF chief alarmed at ‘slow-moving tsunami’ of AI for jobs, taxes
article:
(Oct 12): The head of the International Monetary Fund has warned of the disruptive threat from artificial intelligence to the labour market and taxation, urging policymakers to rethink education and act now to help society adapt.

“It is a slow-moving tsunami, but tsunami nonetheless," managing director Kristalina Georgieva said Monday during her first appearance at the annual meetings of the IMF and World Bank in Bangkok.

Speaking at a session on AI’s impact on employment, she said the technology is already hollowing out demand for many human workers by taking over routine, repetitive tasks. At the same time, it’s increasing low-paying jobs in sectors like construction, which she said is “not a story to celebrate".

It’s a transformation with far-reaching consequences for public finances, Georgieva said. The risk is that AI strains government revenues by tilting the economy toward capital and away from labour — traditionally the main source of tax income.

The comments are the latest warning about the potential shock from AI on jobs and the global economy. Young workers in AI-exposed fields have already seen a slowdown in hiring, leaving new entry-level applicants far more vulnerable. Concern is also growing that the technology will widen inequality, with its gains so far concentrated among a narrow set of workers and economies despite a global investment supercycle.

“We cannot today imagine what exactly the world of work will be five years from now,” she said. “But we can be disciplined and carefully assess what is happening, and then draw lessons, but — most importantly — act on them now.”

See also: Microsoft CEO Nadella calls for ‘emergency brake’ on advanced AI

Despite the employment headwinds, the technology can ultimately prove a positive for growth overall. The IMF estimates the spread of AI can add up to a percentage point to growth in advanced Asian economies.

Such a growth boost “is a very big deal", Georgieva said, adding it will “more than offset” the drag from ageing in rich countries across the region.

title: Wheat extends drop as Trump remarks fuel Black Sea truce hopes
article:
(Oct 12): Wheat declined for a fourth day after US President Donald Trump said Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an immediate “energy ceasefire", raising hopes that an easing of hostilities could reduce Black Sea disruptions.

Futures fell as much as 1.3% in Chicago before paring some losses. Russia and Ukraine together account for more than a quarter of global wheat exports, making the Black Sea critical to world supplies. The US Department of Agriculture unexpectedly raising corn output forecasts also pressured grain prices.

“The energy component isn’t necessarily why; just the general theme of de-escalation is weighing on the market," said Joe Davis, director of commodity sales at Futures International LLC.

Escalating hostilities and strikes on port infrastructure in recent weeks have severely disrupted shipments, forcing buyers from Asia to Africa to seek alternative supplies, often over longer routes and at higher premiums.

Trump announced the truce on Sunday but provided few details. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country supports the ceasefire but is “awaiting details". Traders will be watching for confirmation from Moscow and Kyiv and signs that the agreement could lead to a broader easing of hostilities.

See also: Copper gains on easing rate-hike bets and Chile mine avalanche

A sustained reduction in hostilities could remove some of wheat’s geopolitical risk premium, particularly if shipping becomes safer and Black Sea exports recover. Still, an energy ceasefire wouldn’t automatically protect grain infrastructure or commercial vessels, leaving the outlook for shipments uncertain.

Bearish signals from the USDA are also weighing on grain prices, Davis said. “And with harvest pressure for the next month, it’s going to be hard to rally.”

Corn posted its biggest drop in three years on Friday after the USDA raised its yield and production forecasts for the country’s top crop. The selloff spilled into wheat, which fell as much as 3.2%.

title: South Korean won hits two-year high on lower oil, dollar sales
article:
(Oct 12): South Korea’s won jumped to a two-year high on Monday, supported by lower oil prices and heavy dollar selling by local companies.

The currency rose as much as 0.8% to 1,333.30 against the dollar after the markets returned from a three-day-long weekend before trimming its advance to 0.5%. Most regional peers also gained.

“The won is strengthening in line with broad dollar weakness as the euro, pound and yen all gain on lower oil prices,” said Min Gyeong-won, an economist at Woori Bank in Seoul. Dollar sales by exporters, particularly chipmakers, should continue to support the won, though flows are light today, Min added. Thin trading volumes due to Japan’s holiday are also fuelling volatility.

The Korean won has risen 7.7% this year, swinging from Asia’s worst-performing currency in the first half to its best in the second on strong exports and corporate dollar selling.

title: Copper gains on easing rate-hike bets and Chile mine avalanche
article:
(Oct 12): Copper extended gains as traders looked to a more hopeful outlook for interest rates and gauged the impact on supply of a fatal mine incident in Chile.

The bellwether metal climbed as much as 0.6% on Monday as a fall in oil prices fuelled some optimism that central banks could hold off on further rate hikes to rein in energy-led inflation. This came even as investors weighed geopolitical risks stemming from an escalation in hostilities in the Middle East and while awaiting the mid-week release of US inflation data. Higher borrowing costs typically reduce the appeal of non-yielding commodities.

In Chile, two workers died on Sunday after a snow avalanche struck Codelco’s giant El Teniente copper mine, where open-pit operations had already been halted due to bad weather.

That supply setback comes at a time of trade dislocations and growing global demand for the industrial metal. Chinese inventories remain low following a weeklong national holiday while a gauge of import demand reached a four-year high last week in a sign of potential restocking by buyers in the world’s biggest consumer.

Copper rose 0.5% to US$14,618 a tonne on the London Metal Exchange as of 11.54am in Singapore, after gaining almost 2% last week. Aluminium was stable, while zinc was up 0.6%.

title: Healey needs £35 bil to meet UK spending plans, institute says
article:
(Oct 12): UK Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey must find £35 billion (US$46 billion) to meet the Labour government’s spending ambitions, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) warned ahead of the budget later this month.

The closely watched think tank said that while Healey should have more headroom against his fiscal rules than expected, the credibility of the government’s spending plans was still in the balance.

Inflation will squeeze public spending and leave departments underfunded unless the government intervenes, according to the group. “If you want to put up spending and not squeeze public services, then you have to look at tax rises,” said IFS director Helen Miller.

It came as Healey reaffirmed his commitment to fiscal discipline, as he prepared to travel to Thailand for the 2026 annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund where he will call on allies to work together to limit the impact of global shocks such as the war in the Middle East.

“I will work with our international partners to keep trade moving, support families and businesses, and make Britain’s economy stronger,” Healey said in an emailed statement. “My budget will build on this approach with fiscal discipline helping to deliver economic resilience.”

See also: China moves to stave off wider EU trade war with hybrid deal

Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government is faced with resolving a cost-of-living crisis marked by rising inflation and higher borrowing costs. Healey is due to deliver the budget, the government’s first, on Oct. 28.

The IFS said price pressures will erode the cash value of spending settlements agreed in 2025. Last year’s review implied a £9 billion cut for departments excluding health and defence, and inflation threatens to drive an additional £15 billion hole in those plans. Getting defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, as the government has suggested it wants, would cost a further £11 billion.

Miller said the £35 billion bill could be met by scaling back ambitions for public services but “if you are thinking of tens of billions in spending then you should be doing tens of billions in tax.” One option would be “contingent tax rises” that would be triggered if the economy hasn’t improved by a set time.

See also: Rich countries are now on front lines as world’s risk map shifts

A tax-raising measure being mooted by Healey was to cut the threshold on the “mansion tax,” an annual levy charged on high-value homes, from £2 million to £1.5 million. But one person familiar with the Treasury’s thinking said such a move was no longer likely, after Labour MPs warned the chancellor that it would damage Labour’s ratings in its central London strongholds. The shift was first reported by the Sunday Times.

The forecast did offer Healey some relief. The chancellor’s cushion against fiscal rules he inherited has fallen only slightly, to £21 billion.

He is planning a budget that gives households and business “breathing space” after two earlier budgets added £66 billion in taxes and borrowing rose. Healey has promised fiscal discipline and investors have signalled they would tolerate headroom of as little as £15 billion.

“The headroom isn’t going to tell you whether the plan to get borrowing down is credible,” Miller said. “For that, you’re going to need to judge whether the spending plans are credible.” She added that “simply pencilling in implicit cuts” with no intention of delivering them “would make the budget a work of fiction.”

The IFS teamed up with Barclays Plc for the think tank’s annual Green Budget analysis of the current economic challenges, alongside which it publishes updated fiscal forecasts. Earlier estimates by economists suggested the government’s headroom against its main rule that taxes must cover day-to-day spending in 2029-30 would halve to about £12 billion, leaving Healey with a set of difficult decisions to restore the buffer.

However, the IFS and Barclays said a £12 billion hit from higher borrowing costs and £10 billion of extra welfare spending, reflecting the inflation indexing of benefits, would be almost entirely offset by additional tax receipts due to inflation and higher wages.

Miller stressed that there was “huge uncertainty” around the estimates, which could be “£10 billion higher or lower” in the critical 2029-30 financial year.

Barclays chief UK economist Jack Meaning said the market backdrop to the budget was better than in the last two years, when bond investors were spooked by the size of the fiscal events and the thin headroom. The UK “has not been the focus for global bond investors at the moment,” he said.

title: DBS CEO Tan says market repricing risks on AI financing
article:
(Oct 12): The market is repricing the risks around investments related to the buildup of artificial intelligence that could lead to more discipline in financing, according to DBS Group Holdings Ltd chief executive officer Tan Su Shan.

“The market has spoken,” Tan said in an interview with Bloomberg Television on Monday. “It’s not a bad thing because now, people are asking for higher returns, and people are also looking at structures. They’re making sure that whatever money is now being hoovered into the whole AI capex ecosystem will lead to some kind of long-term ROI that can then be repaid back to debt or bond or equity holders.”

Tan, who leads Southeast Asia’s biggest lender, said weaker firms may see their credit ratings revised downwards, though this risk repricing is “healthy” as the market wants to make sure that big financial commitments are sustainable.

Her comments come as technology giants spend billions on AI, and as market gains concentrate in a handful of stocks. Interest rates are rising and bond yields around the world have surged to the highest in decades, increasing the cost of funding the enormous investment needed to build AI infrastructure. PricewaterhouseCoopers LLP estimates Asia’s spending on data centres could reach US$8.2 trillion ($10.5 trillion) by 2050.

DBS has originated about S$25 billion of AI deals this year, often as lead manager on syndicated loans and has held only a fraction of that, Tan said. The financing is mostly for hardware, from semiconductors and memory chips to data centres, she added.

Tan was speaking on the sidelines of DBS’ conference that focuses on key topics like AI and geopolitics, and features speakers including TikTok Inc’s CEO Shou Chew, Intel Corp’s CEO Lip-Bu Tan and Broadcom Inc’s CEO Hock Tan. In her opening comments, Tan said she hasn’t seen this kind of volatility in interest rates for a long time, with equity investors whipsawed by swings in AI stocks.

See also: DOJ scrutinises Binance compliance with 2023 settlement deal

Tan also said conflicts in the Middle East and involving Russia were escalating at a pace that has become worrying. “Frankly, I find it exhausting just to look at so much tension and so much stress in the system,” she said.

Tan has made AI key to her strategy since taking the helm in March last year. The Singapore-based bank is starting to see results from large AI projects that are underway to overhaul its work flows and proccesses, and these include fee growth and new accounts being opened at a faster pace, she said.

Meanwhile, Tan also said the wealth management business has long term structural tailwinds as Asia creates more wealth, the capital markets deepen and intergenerational wealth transfer happens. While market swings will affect flows in the short term, net new money growth has been “consistently strong,” she added.

title: China moves to stave off wider EU trade war with hybrid deal
article:
(Oct 12): With an agreement to curb exports of hybrid vehicles to the European Union, China is betting it can sidestep harsher restrictions from the 27-member bloc with a gesture that has little immediate prospect of reshaping the overall trade relationship.

Talks between China and the EU ended late Friday with a 16-point consensus spanning trade and investment, export controls and intellectual property rights. The EU said China agreed to slash millions of hybrid car exports, with people familiar with discussions saying the bloc intends to use safeguard measures to curb the imports.

EU leaders meet on Thursday to decide whether to adopt a more forceful response to the surge in Chinese exports, which threaten to hollow out European manufacturing industries and decimate millions of jobs. Germany and France last week called for stronger tools — including an instrument that could cut off China from the bloc’s massive single market — to defend sectors hit by surging subsidized Chinese imports.

The agreement on Friday buys time for further negotiations, with the two sides planning for more talks in January and March, said Joe Peissel, lead macroeconomist at research firm Trivium China. He called it a strategic win for China, saying in a research note that “Beijing has played a blinder.”

“In exchange for reviews, dialogue, and ‘understandings,’ it has conceded little on the structural drivers of the EU’s massive trade deficit,” he wrote. “Beyond vehicles and modest tariff relief, nothing in the 16-point agreement suggests a significant rewiring of China’s trading terms with the EU.”

See also: Rich countries are now on front lines as world’s risk map shifts

EU leaders are seeking ways to stop China from flooding the continent with goods that have led to a trade deficit now exceeding €1 billion (US$1.1 billion or $1.4 billion) a day. Weak consumption at home has left China increasingly reliant on a world-beating manufacturing sector and overseas demand to support its sluggish domestic economy.

China’s Ministry of Commerce on Friday said the two sides reaffirmed their commitment as key trading partners to properly manage differences under World Trade Organization rules. They also agreed to maintain stable bilateral economic and trade ties while making them “more balanced.”

Friday’s joint statement said the two sides had reached an “understanding on trade in hybrid vehicles in a WTO compliant manner.” Chinese hybrid car sales have escalated in part because they escaped the EU’s 2024 tariffs on electric vehicles. In August, Chinese car brands accounted for about a quarter of European hybrid sales.

See also: Egypt inflation slows again despite Iran war price pressures

The EU will cap the import of Chinese hybrid vehicles at 350,000 cars per year, according to a document outlining the plan and seen by Bloomberg News, a measure taking effect as soon as Dec 1.

The 350,000 car limit will apply for the first year of the cap, then will increase by 6% annually from the second year of application, according to the document. The measures will apply for four years, during which time both countries will pledge to abide by World Trade Organization rules.

Safeguard measures planned by the EU typically take the form of tariff-rate quotas, which apply a levy on imports above a certain volume to curb excess flows. That would comply with WTO rules — something both China and the EU have said is a requirement.

EU ambassadors briefed by trade chief Maros Sefcovic on Sunday broadly welcomed the result while stressing that they viewed it as just the beginning of the process to rebalance the trade relationship, according to people familiar with the talks, who spoke on the condition of anonymity. The goal is for the EU safeguard measures to apply from Dec 1.

Chinese carmakers like Chery Automobile Co. have massively stepped up vehicle shipments to the EU in response to a slump in their home market, exacerbating a deceleration plaguing European peers, which are among the worst-performing globally. Mercedes-Benz Group AG car sales dropped by 8% in the third quarter, while Volkswagen AG last month slashed its profit forecast following a similar warning from BMW AG in June.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Renault SA chief executive officer Francois Provost called the deal with China a “major milestone” that will help foster a future for Europe’s automotive industry. He was among business leaders who met with Sefcovic ahead of his trip to China for the talks.

“I had urged him to seek an agreement quickly,” Provost said in an interview Sunday. “Without one, we would be looking at a trade war with China, which would be a lose-lose situation for everyone.”

The timing of the EU-China agreement “indicates that China is keen to ease tensions” before the bloc’s leaders meet, said Henry Gao, a law professor at Singapore Management University. “Given its ongoing trade frictions with the United States, Beijing is unlikely to want a simultaneous escalation with Europe.”

“If the EU insists on strictly WTO-consistent approaches, such measures may not be particularly effective in addressing the surge of Chinese exports, as past cases have demonstrated,” Gao added. “WTO-compliant trade remedies can provide some relief, but they are often limited in scope and may not significantly alter broader trade flows.”

France and Germany have called on the EU to investigate whether subsidized imports are harming sectors like chemicals and plastics — probes that could produce more tariffs. The proposal was seen as a pressure tactic targeting Beijing, putting Germany’s weight behind forceful moves it had previously opposed.

“It has taken a tremendous amount of political capital for European officials to get this far on autos, and it’s not clear that the approach could be easily copy-pasted to other industries,” said Christopher Beddor, deputy China research director at Gavekal Dragonomics.

Beijing has preemptively warned the EU against adopting what it called protectionist measures. China’s dominance of critical rare earth supplies — leverage it’s already wielded in trade negotiations with the US — gives Beijing a powerful deterrent as Europe simultaneously tries to curb Chinese imports and secure the materials its factories need.

“Sweeping trade barriers and tariffs would probably incur retaliation from Beijing, and Chinese officials have the nuclear option of threatening to restrict rare-earths exports,” Beddor said. “But at this stage, they seem more inclined to cut a deal.”

title: Amazon in talks to buy AI startup Decart, WSJ reports
article:
(Oct 12): Amazon.com Inc is in negotiations to acquire Decart AI, an artificial intelligence startup, in a deal that could be valued at around US$7 billion, the Wall Street Journal reported.

The purchase could be wrapped up soon if the negotiations don’t collapse, the Journal said, citing people familiar with the matter.

In September, Anthropic decided against acquiring Decart AI. The Claude chatbot maker had been in talks to buy Decart for about US$6 billion and had performed due diligence on the target.

Decart was founded in 2023 by three Israeli engineers, brothers Dean and Orian Leitersdorf and Moshe Shalev.

title: Beng Kuang reports $71.5 mil orderbook for 9MFY2026
article:
In a bourse filing on Oct 12, offshore and marine services and equipment provider Beng Kuang Marine has updated that its order book stood at around $71.5 million as at 9MFY2026 ended Sept 31.

Approximately 84% of the orderbook or $59.8 million is from subsidiary Asian Sealand Offshore and Marine (ASOM), with the remainder coming from other subsidiaries PT. Nexus Engineering Indonesia (NEI) and International Offshore Equipments Pte Ltd (IOE).

For the third quarter, ASOM secured $27.2 million in orders, bringing 9MFY2026 total to $112.4 million. ASOM’s contracts and purchase orders includes maintenance and tank-services frameworks supporting life-extension programmes for 19 floating, production, storage and offloading (FPSO) and floating, storage and offloading (FSO) vessels, with execution remaining subject to contractual terms and operator requirements. In May, Beng Kuang acquired the remaining 49% stake of ASOM it did not own.

NEI and IOE continue delivery of their respective engineering and equipment projects, the filing updates.

“Underpinned by FPSO operators’ long-term focus on production reliability, ASOM’s contracted workload supports our continued focus on FPSO lifecycle services,” says CEO Yong Jiunn Run. “The additional tank-services award this quarter, alongside the life-extension frameworks announced in the first half, illustrates how ongoing customer maintenance needs translate into successive work scopes.”

Shares in Beng Kuang closed at 37 cents on Oct 9. Ytd, the counter is up around 15%.

title: Oil rises on Mideast attacks, dollar edges high
article:
(Oct 12) : Oil advanced while the dollar edged higher in early Asian trading as investors weighed escalating Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and the risk of a widening Middle East conflict.

Global benchmark Brent crude advanced 0.4% to US$105.10 a barrel. The dollar was slightly stronger against major peers, while the risk-sensitive Australian dollar was steady. S&P 500 futures gained after the underlying gauge closed 0.6% higher in New York on Friday. Cash Treasury trading is closed for holidays in the US and Japan.

Saudi Arabia’s main airport came under renewed Houthi attack Sunday, a day after a strike killed 12 people, raising the risk of a broader conflict that may draw in the US and further disrupt energy supplies and global trade. The escalation comes as Saudi Arabia backs a counteroffensive near Bab el-Mandeb, a critical shipping chokepoint between Asia and Europe.

The attacks threaten to inject fresh volatility into a pivotal week for markets, with inflation data due in the US and Europe and a host of central bank officials scheduled to speak. Further disruption to energy supplies may add to price pressures and bolster expectations for higher interest rates.

“In quieter conditions, geopolitical headlines can often have an outsized impact,” Nick Twidale, chief market analyst at AT Global Markets in Sydney, wrote in a note to clients. But with the US inflation reading, several central bank speakers and the start of another US earnings season this week, “there will be plenty for markets to digest,” he wrote.

Traders are looking to the latest US consumer-price data due this week and a scheduled appearance by Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh for clues on the pace of further interest-rate increases. A stronger-than-expected September inflation reading may rekindle the recent bond selloff by putting pressure on the Fed to tighten policy more aggressively.

See also: Bond selloff may mean fewer rate hikes from global central banks

The 10-year Treasury yield approached 5.4% last week, its highest since 2002, as Brent crude traded above US$100 a barrel and fueled concern that elevated energy costs may prolong inflation pressures.

Equities, meanwhile, have largely weathered the turmoil. The S&P 500 hit a record Tuesday before retreating over the next two sessions on concerns about AI demand, then rebounded Friday as investors turned toward another strong earnings season. The gauge remains within striking distance of its peak.

Investors will be watching for signs that higher costs are squeezing margins even as corporate America enjoys one of its strongest profit cycles in years. The S&P 500 has recorded seven consecutive quarters of double-digit earnings growth, and analysts expect third-quarter profits to rise roughly 25% from a year earlier, according to data compiled by Bloomberg Intelligence.

See also: US bond traders await CPI, Warsh for insight on Fed’s rate path

Elsewhere, the dollar traded in a narrow range against major peers after posting a fourth straight weekly gain, its longest winning streak since early 2025. Elevated oil prices and the war with Iran have supported the greenback as investors sought safety.

Speculative traders remain bullish on the dollar, betting the US economy is better placed than its major peers to withstand further interest-rate increases. Fiscal concerns in France and elevated energy prices have weighed on the euro, which touched its lowest since May 2025 last week, providing additional support for the greenback.

“The case for US dollar to break out of its 15-month range is increasingly compelling,” Barclays strategists led by Themistoklis Fiotakis wrote in a note to clients. “US growth outperformance, limited scope for lower yields and Europe’s fiscal and energy vulnerabilities point to further upside. However, stretched long positioning could interrupt the rally in the near term.”

title: Bond selloff may mean fewer rate hikes from global central banks
article:
(Oct 12) : Bond markets are starting to do some of the lifting for central banks around the world by pushing up borrowing costs themselves, potentially reducing the number of benchmark interest-rate hikes needed to get inflation under control.

Yields have surged to multiyear highs after weeks of selling, tightening financial conditions even without further action from policymakers. Traders have responded by paring rate-hike expectations, with the amount priced into swaps across eight major economies falling by almost 200 basis points since mid-September, according to data compiled by Bloomberg.

There are few signs the bond selloff is abating as concerns over fiscal spending from the US to Japan and France push investors to demand more compensation, while a slew of AI-related debt issuance soaks up capital.

The higher borrowing costs are spilling into mortgages and junk credit, delivering some of the economic restraint central banks would otherwise seek through higher policy rates.

“The more tightening markets price, the tighter financial conditions become,” said Ken Orchard, head of international fixed income at T. Rowe Price, which oversees US$1.9 trillion. “And the tighter financial conditions become, the less tightening central banks may ultimately need — or be able — to deliver.”

Traders are now pricing in a combined 539 basis points of rate hikes across the eight economies, down from 717 basis points in September, when expectations were the highest since 2022, data compiled by Bloomberg show. The biggest pullback has been in Australia, followed by the euro area amid concerns over France’s fiscal outlook, then South Korea and Canada.

See also: US bond traders await CPI, Warsh for insight on Fed’s rate path

The average yield on global government bonds has climbed above 4% to the highest since 2000, raising the question of where the tipping point lies. Higher yields may do some of central banks’ work for them, but if they appear too focused on bolstering growth, investors may doubt their commitment to fighting inflation and demand an even bigger premium to hold longer-dated debt.

“Central banks would ultimately have to balance the growth mandate with near-term inflation risk,” said Yuxuan Tang, Asia head of rates and foreign-exchange strategy at JPMorgan Private Bank. “We think most rates markets are now overpricing the risk of further hikes, given the increasing downside risks to growth from the war’s repercussions.”

For investors, that may make bonds look attractive again. High-quality fixed income is a buy because they remain one of the best hedges against inflation and a slowdown in growth, Tang said, adding that the sharp rise in yields over the past month has materially improved the risk-reward trade-off.

See also: Asian stocks set to fall on tech, oil edges lower

Deutsche Bank AG is now seeing opportunities in US Treasuries. “Our view is that at least from an energy perspective, this situation won’t stay forever,” said Christian Nolting, its global chief investment officer for private banking based in Frankfurt. “The energy situation will get better and inflation is coming down. And from that perspective, I don’t think we are in a full hiking cycle.”

Barclays Plc strategists say markets have already taken some of the pressure off the Federal Reserve. “Some of the tightening has occurred independently of expectations for additional Fed hikes,” they wrote. “All else equal, that should reduce the urgency for the Fed to raise rates, even if the risk-management framework leaves the bias toward further tightening intact.”

Not everyone is convinced. Some say markets are still underpricing the risk of hikes, with the war prolonging inflation pressure through elevated oil prices. Oil remains above US$100 a barrel as traders weigh Iran’s escalating attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz against President Donald Trump’s comments that the US would “not be attacking” Tehran before November’s midterm elections.

Even if damage to growth becomes harder to ignore and central banks pause, fiscal concerns may limit the drop in longer-dated yields, according to Kenneth Goh, director of private wealth management at UOB Kay Hian in Singapore.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has sought to reassure skeptical investors, saying stronger growth and spending restraint will “very quickly” improve the trajectory of US borrowing. In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said her administration is prepared to review spending and revenue plans if bond yields move unexpectedly.

Yields on US 10-year Treasuries have jumped more than 70 basis points since the start of the second half, while equivalent yields in Japan have risen 31 basis points and those in Germany and France have climbed 61 and 121 basis points, respectively.

For now, policymakers are signaling they’re prepared to act. Fed officials voted unanimously last month to raise their benchmark rate for the first time since July 2023, although some have advocated flexibility in a sign they may not act again this month. India has turned more hawkish, with the Reserve Bank raising rates for the first time in nearly four years and signaling further tightening ahead.

That backdrop will loom over the International Monetary Fund’s annual meetings in Bangkok starting Monday, where global policymakers will focus on growth, inflation, rates and government debt. Wednesday’s release of the US’s consumer price index for September will also be closely watched for clues on the Fed’s rate path.

title: US bond traders await CPI, Warsh for insight on Fed’s rate path
article:
(Oct 12) : Bond traders are looking to the latest consumer-price inflation figures and a planned appearance by Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh for insight into how quickly the central bank will continue raising interest rates.

After a sharp jump in the wake of the Fed’s unanimous rate hike last month, Treasury yields were little changed last week, hovering around a 24-year high as investors wait for new data.

The bond selloff was restrained by the significant slowdown in job growth shown in this month’s employment report, which lead traders to anticipate that the Fed will hold steady at its next meeting in late October. They continue to anticipate a quarter-point increase in December, followed by two more by late 2027.

The positioning is raising the risk that a bigger-than-expected increase in the consumer price index in September will rekindle the selloff by putting pressure on the Fed to raise rates more aggressively.

“The risk to the CPI report is asymmetric, as a hotter print could signal that the Fed may need to pick up the pace of tightening, while a weaker, or at consensus print continues to feed into the Fed exercising caution going forward,” said Molly Brooks, US rates strategist at TD Securities.

Warsh will speak Thursday in a discussion at the International Monetary Fund’s annual meeting in Bangkok, Thailand. Two other closely followed Fed officials, governor Christopher Waller and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack, are also speaking. The central bank will start observing its usual communications blackout from Saturday, ahead of the two day meeting that ends on Oct. 28.

See also: Asian stocks set to fall on tech, oil edges lower

“This will be the last week before blackout period, so Fedspeak post CPI” will help markets have “less uncertainty” about the outcome of the next meeting, said Brooks. She said, “Warsh is likely to continue to shy away from forward guidance, which the market is expecting.”

The consumer price index will be released Wednesday. Economists expect it to rise 0.6% from the month before, up from 0.4% previously. The core measure, which strips out volatile food and energy prices, is seen easing to 0.2% from 0.3%, according to a Bloomberg survey of economists. Both year-over-year measures are forecast higher, with headline figure seen running at a 3.6% pace and the core reading at 2.5%.

The bond market will be closed Monday for a public holiday. US equities will remain open for trading.
